exploration.title: Moving Plates
exploration.subject: Earth science
exploration.summary: Compare spreading, oceanic–continental subduction and transform motion at equal rates and times, then test a bounded locked-fault illustration.
exploration.question: How does the direction plates move change what happens at their boundary?
exploration.explanation: A tectonic plate is lithosphere: crust plus rigid uppermost mantle. It moves over hotter, slowly deforming, mostly solid asthenosphere. At a divergent mid-ocean ridge, oceanic lithosphere separates and localized melt can cool into new oceanic crust. In this oceanic–continental convergent example, denser oceanic lithosphere bends beneath continental lithosphere at a trench; melt is localized in the mantle wedge above the slab, not throughout the mantle or entire slab. At a transform boundary, plates move horizontally past one another without creating or destroying crust in this model. The calculation assumes a constant relative rate: 1 cm/yr sustained for 1 million years gives 10 km of relative motion. That arithmetic is exact for the displayed units, but the chosen rates, times, scene dimensions, relief and slab angle are teaching inputs rather than a reconstruction of a named plate boundary. The separate locked-fault illustration uses an invented five-step threshold and 20-slip display limit. It has no time or magnitude scale and cannot predict an earthquake date, location, magnitude or hazard.

experiments.title: Boundary direction
experiments.instruction: Predict first. Compare Apart and Together at 4 cm/yr for 2.0 million years. Change only the boundary example; hold rate, elapsed time and schematic view fixed.
experiments.observe: Both examples calculate 80 km of relative motion. Apart forms a ridge and new oceanic crust; Together forms a trench and carries oceanic lithosphere beneath continental lithosphere. Explain why equal relative motion can build different structures.

experiments.title: Locked fault slip
experiments.instruction: Predict first. Start Sideways after four equal loading steps, then add only the fifth step. Hold the boundary, long-term rate and elapsed model time fixed.
experiments.observe: The invented loading index drops from 80% to 0%, the illustrated slip count changes from 0 to 1 and the surface marker gains one schematic offset. Explain why this timeless five-step illustration is not an earthquake clock or hazard forecast.

exploration.misconception: Tectonic plates are not crust alone, and the mantle is not a global ocean of liquid magma. Plates continue moving between earthquakes; earthquakes can occur at all boundary types and within plates. A regular schematic slip sequence is not a real earthquake clock.
